title: Never Underestimate the Houthis
gist: Alexandra Stark argues the Houthis are a pragmatic, self-interested actor, not an Iranian proxy, and with Iran effectively closing Hormuz they can choke the Bab al-Mandab/Red Sea–Suez route. Renewed attacks on Saudi tankers, infrastructure and the Yanbu workaround threaten a dual chokepoint closure that would push oil prices and inflation higher. A US–Iran deal will not bind them.

themes.theme: Dual chokepoint risk: Hormuz plus Bab al-Mandab

insights.claim: 12–15% of maritime trade passes through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea that the Houthis can disrupt because of geography.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: A large share of global shipping is exposed to a single non-state actor.
insights.quote: through which 12 percent to 15 percent of maritime trade travels.
insights.locator: Perhaps they were biding their time.

insights.claim: With Iran effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis are now in an unusually powerful position over the remaining Red Sea–Suez route for oil and LNG to North American and European markets.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: The Houthis now control the marginal route for Gulf energy exports.
insights.quote: With Iran effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis are now in an unusually powerful position.
insights.locator: Perhaps they were biding their time.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia had bypassed Hormuz by piping crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, but the new Houthi attacks have disrupted that option.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Saudi crude bypass capacity is compromised, which tightens effective oil supply.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia had sought to avoid Hormuz by routing crude oil via a pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu on its western coast. The new Houthi attacks have disrupted that option.
insights.locator: With the effective closure of Hormuz

insights.claim: Near-closure of both the Hormuz and Suez routes could compound trade problems and push oil prices and inflation even higher.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Upside risk for oil prices, freight and inflation prints.
insights.quote: The near closure of both Hormuz and the Suez routes could compound problems for global trade, pushing the cost of oil and inflation even higher.
insights.locator: With the effective closure of Hormuz

insights.claim: The 2023–25 Houthi attacks had a significant but ultimately manageable global economic effect with small inflation impact, but closing Bab al-Mandab at the same time as Hormuz would likely be more dire.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Don't anchor on the benign 2023–25 inflation precedent; the combined shock is nonlinear.
insights.quote: The economic effects of closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the same time as Hormuz are likely to be more dire.
insights.locator: The previous round of Houthi attacks

insights.claim: In 2023 the Houthis used low-cost drones, missiles and unmanned surface vessels to raise commercial ship insurance costs as much as twentyfold, effectively closing the strait.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Cheap asymmetric weapons can shut a major lane by repricing risk.
insights.quote: driving up the cost of insuring commercial ships as much as twentyfold, effectively closing the strait.

insights.claim: The only alternative route, around the southern tip of Africa, adds 4,000 or more nautical miles and raises shipping costs.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Rerouting lengthens voyages and raises freight costs.

insights.claim: In the latest round, commercial ships still transit the Red Sea, but tanker traffic has fallen substantially over the past month; an Aug. 12 attack on a cargo ship caused the round's first reported fatalities.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Tanker flows are already falling, an early indicator of further escalation.
insights.quote: For now, commercial ships continue to transit the Red Sea, although tanker traffic has declined substantially over the past month.

insights.claim: The Houthis resumed Red Sea attacks, striking Saudi-linked oil tankers and Saudi energy and transport infrastructure, in response to alleged Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa Airport's runway on July 13.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Direct threat to Saudi energy assets and export logistics.

insights.claim: The Houthis have also claimed attacks on a ship at the Red Sea port of Mokha and on airports and oil refinery infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Saudi refining is exposed, a risk for product markets.

insights.claim: The Houthis appear to see an opening either to gain leverage in negotiations with Saudi Arabia over a Yemen settlement or to resume attacks on the internationally backed government.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: The Yemen civil war could reignite, drawing in Saudi Arabia.

insights.claim: While the US tries to wind down the war with Iran, the Houthis threaten to restart the Yemen war, which would likely draw in Saudi Arabia, menace global oil trade and keep the region unstable.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: A regional ceasefire with Iran may not end the energy-supply risk.

themes.theme: Houthis are not an Iranian proxy

insights.claim: Although the Houthis benefit from Iranian weapons, training and know-how, they act on their own interests rather than as a subsidiary of Tehran.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Deals with Tehran won't automatically de-risk the Red Sea.
insights.quote: while they benefit from Iranian weapons, training and know-how, the Houthis also have their own interests at heart—and behave accordingly.

insights.claim: A key assumption behind the US–Israeli attack on Iran from February was that Iran's proxies were critically weakened; the Houthis stayed out at first, may have been biding their time, and avoided similar damage.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: The 'weakened axis' consensus underestimated a residual actor.

insights.claim: The Houthis are savvy about when to escalate: their 2023–25 shipping attacks were framed as pressure on Israel over Gaza but also shored up domestic legitimacy and diverted attention from governance failures.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: Domestic incentives make Houthi escalation more likely when they are weak at home.
insights.quote: The strikes also bolstered their legitimacy in the territory they control in northern Yemen, diverting attention from their governance failures
insights.locator: Highly attuned to their own interests

insights.claim: No one should assume a deal with Iran will bind the Houthis; de-escalation requires confronting them directly as a pragmatic, dangerous, self-interested actor.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Stark
insights.so_what: An Iran deal is not a full de-risking signal for Red Sea shipping or oil.
insights.quote: no one should assume that a deal with Iran will bind what the Houthis do next.
insights.locator: It will be difficult to de-escalate
